intro: Westonbirt, The National Arboretum, sits about 5 km south-west of Tetbury in Gloucestershire, roughly 27 km north-east of Bath and 31 km from Bristol in a straight line, and a car is the realistic way in. Its oldest tree is not one of the famous plantings but a small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, coppiced for centuries and claimed at 2,000 years. In the Old Arboretum stand giant redwoods, the oldest documented pair planted in 1856, and one tree that has rooted its own branches into a ring of new trees.
meta_description: A small-leaved lime in Silk Wood claimed at 2,000 years and kept alive by coppicing, beside the 1856 gateway redwoods of Westonbirt Arboretum.
question_meta: Westonbirt Arboretum's oldest tree is a small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, claimed at 2,000 years and kept alive by coppicing. What is known and what is not.
question_answer: The oldest tree at Westonbirt Arboretum is the small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, which Forestry England calls the 2,000-year-old lime. It is a ring of about 60 coppice stems from one ancient stool, last cut in November 2012. Nobody has dated it, so the 2,000 years is the owner's estimate rather than a measurement.
question_context: A small-leaved lime normally lives about 500 years, according to the Friends of Westonbirt. This one has outlasted that, they say, because it has been coppiced again and again. Cut to the base every twenty years or so, it sends up a fresh ring of stems from the old roots. Forestry England describes the original tree as thought to be hundreds, possibly thousands, of years old, and coppicing in Silk Wood is recorded from 1292. The 2,000 figure is repeated by both the owner and the Friends but rests on no dating study, so treat it as a strong tradition. The lime's 2012 coppice became a sculpture by Richard Harris, and the next cut is due around 2032. Do not expect a tower. What you will find is a thicket of poles that happens to be one very old tree. The arboretum's other big names are younger and better documented. The giant redwoods at the original gateway were planted in 1856, according to Redwood World citing the Forestry Commission, and by 2010 the taller of them stood 38 metres.

faq.q: How do I get to Westonbirt from Bath or Bristol?
faq.a: Westonbirt is off the A433 about 5 km south-west of Tetbury, roughly 27 km north-east of Bath and 31 km from Bristol in a straight line. The nearest station is Kemble, about 12 km away, so a car or taxi is the realistic route. The arboretum offers discounted entry to visitors arriving by bus, train or bike.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to see the trees?
faq.a: Yes. Westonbirt charges for entry, about 14 to 22 GBP for an adult day ticket depending on season and day on its 2026 pages. It opens daily from 9am except Christmas Day, with last admission at 4pm, and booking ahead is advised in autumn.
Dogs on leads are allowed in Silk Wood, where the old lime stands, but not in the Old Arboretum, where the redwoods are.

trees.name: The 2,000-year-old lime of Silk Wood

location.address: Silk Wood, Westonbirt Arboretum, near Tetbury, Gloucestershire GL8 8QS

trees.story:
Every twenty years Westonbirt cuts this tree to the ground, and that is how it has stayed alive. The small-leaved lime in Silk Wood is not one trunk but a ring of about 60 stems, all rising from a single ancient stool. Forestry England, which owns the arboretum, calls it the 2,000-year-old lime and describes the original tree as thought to be hundreds, possibly thousands, of years old. Nobody has dated it. The 2,000 is an estimate repeated by the owner and the Friends of Westonbirt, not a measurement, so read it as a tradition with a good argument behind it.

The argument is the axe. Left alone, a small-leaved lime usually lives about 500 years, the Friends say. Cut back to its base, it sends up fresh stems from the old roots, and continuous coppicing is their explanation for why this one has outlived that span. Coppicing in Silk Wood is recorded as far back as 1292, so the practice that keeps this tree going has more than seven centuries on the record in this wood alone.

The last harvest came in November 2012, and the poles were built into a sculpture by Richard Harris. On a twenty-year rotation, the next cut falls around 2032. Come expecting a thicket rather than a tower. What looks like a clump of young poles is the visible top of something very old.

Friends of Westonbirt members enter free. The lime stands in Silk Wood, the ancient coppice woodland part of the site; dogs on leads are allowed in Silk Wood but not the Old Arboretum.

trees.name: The entrance redwoods of Mitchell Drive

location.address: Original entrance at the end of Mitchell Drive, Old Arboretum, Westonbirt Arboretum, near Tetbury GL8 8QS

trees.story:
In 1856 Mr and Mrs Holford planted two giant redwood saplings a foot tall either side of their arboretum's gateway, at 8 pounds each. That is the account Redwood World gives, citing the Forestry Commission; we have not seen the owner's own record, so the date stands on one source.

What is not in doubt is what the saplings became. When Redwood World measured them in September 2010, the taller stood 38 metres with a trunk 6.97 metres round at chest height, and its partner reached 34 metres and 5.27 metres. Both have had another sixteen years of growth since. They stand about ten metres apart at the end of Mitchell Drive, framing what was the original way into Westonbirt, and from the drive they still read as a deliberate pair.

The pair have outgrown the gateway in one literal way. The root of the tree beside the wall has pushed up the ground and lifted the middle of the wall with it, a slow piece of demolition by a tree that was planted to decorate it.

They have watched the Old Arboretum fill in around them for 170 years, from a planting by one family to a national collection that takes paying visitors every day of the year but one.

trees.name: The layered redwood of the Old Arboretum

location.address: Old Arboretum, Westonbirt Arboretum, near Tetbury GL8 8QS

trees.story:
This giant redwood is making copies of itself. Its lower branches bent until they touched the ground, put down roots and grew up as new trees, so what you see at the edge of this copse is one tall redwood ringed by its own offspring. Foresters call it layering.

The main stem is big enough to earn the visit on its own. Redwood World measured it in September 2010 at 42.4 metres tall, with a trunk 6.78 metres round at chest height. Two metres away stands a second stem, 41.2 metres and 6.45 metres round, close enough that we treat the two as one stop.

What nobody has written down is when it was planted. The Old Arboretum's oldest redwoods at the gateway are documented from 1856, but there is no record that ties this one to that date, and we will not borrow it. If you know when this group went in, tell us.

All the figures come from that one 2010 survey, so expect the tree to be somewhat taller now. Look for the layered skirt, a redwood that has quietly started a small wood of its own.

trees.name: The stout redwood of the Old Arboretum

location.address: Old Arboretum, Westonbirt Arboretum, near Tetbury GL8 8QS

trees.story:
Of the 51 giant redwoods Redwood World measured in Westonbirt's Old Arboretum in 2010, this one had the thickest waist. Its trunk was 7.01 metres round at chest height, wider than the famous pair at the old gateway and wider than the 42-metre layered tree about 60 metres to the north-east.

It is not the tallest. At 34.2 metres it stood eight metres below the layered tree in that survey, a redwood that has put its growth into girth rather than height.

The arboretum tracks it as tag 02.0142, and the measurements come from a single independent survey taken in September 2010, so the girth today will be somewhat larger. The planting date is the open question. No source we have found says when it went in, and we would rather leave the age blank than guess one from its neighbours. If you have the arboretum's planting record for this tree, tell us.

It makes a good last stop after the layered copse. Walk the 60 metres between them and you have seen a 42-metre redwood and the stoutest one Redwood World recorded here within a few minutes of each other.
